transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-09-12 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Rivera (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Miguel Torres (Redwood SE), Jordan Patel (Lumenix Eng Lead), Sofia Nguyen (PM), Devon Clarke (SRE), Aisha Khan (Security)

Auto-summary: quick hosted API demo focusing on chat/text gen basics, streaming behavior, parameter tuning and retry/fallback strategies; walkthrough of Redwood Console Optimize suggestions; agreed next steps around pilot and security docs.

Topics: 1) how streaming vs chunked responses behave, 2) tokens/latency tradeoffs and param knobs, 3) retry/backoff patterns and idempotency, 4) console quick tour (routes, metrics, Optimize suggestions), 5) security/compliance checklist items for hosted api

[00:00] Alex (AE): All right, thanks everyone for joining. Quick intros then we'll jump into a short demo. Priya and Miguel will handle the deep bits. Jordan, maybe start by telling us your primary success criteria?

[00:20] Jordan (Lumenix): Yeah sure. Main metrics for us are sub-200ms median token latency for short messages (<128 tokens) and stable cost per active user. We're also very sensitive to PII leakage — so data retention settings and audit logs are must-haves.

[00:35] Sofia (PM): And timeline — want a pilot in the next 2 weeks, production in ~2 months if the pilot hits SLAs.

[00:42] Alex: Great, that aligns well with the hosted onramp. Priya, I'll pass to you for the demo.

[00:49] Priya (SE): Cool, thanks. I'm going to share my screen — showing Redwood Console, route config for chat endpoint, and a live sandbox where we can see streaming chunks come in. The key knobs we typically tune are temperature, max_tokens, top_p, and the streaming chunk size. Also batching window and concurrency limits in the console.

[01:20] Miguel (SE): Quick note, when you enable prefix KV caching it reduces repeated context cost a lot for chatbots that keep conversation history. We sometimes call it KV cache but the transcript may say "KV cash" on automated exports.

[01:34] Devon (SRE): How do you handle ordering when streaming partial tokens — any chance of reordering on retries?

[01:40] Priya: Good question. By default we stream progressively and keep a monotonic sequence number per response. If a connection breaks we implement a retry that either restarts from last known token index using KV cache checkpoint or falls back to a stateless re-generation. For idempotency we recommend including a client_message_id so the server can detect duplicates.

[02:10] Sofia: Can you show an SDK example? We're using Node on the front end and Go on the backend.

[02:18] Priya: Sure. (typing) Example snippet: open a streaming connection, include conversation_id and client_message_id, set max_tokens: 64, and set stream_chunk_size to 16. If you see mid-stream errors, the recommended client behavior is exponential backoff with jitter and resume using the checkpoint token offset. We'll paste this snippet into the follow-up repo.

[03:05] Jordan: We care about tail latency too. How does Redwood handle small spikes?

[03:12] Miguel: Two mechanisms — autoscale pools for hosted which absorb sustained load, and a soft burst queue for short spikes. For ultra-low tail latency you can pin to Dedicated GPUs but that is a different contract. The hosted route offers latency SLOs and can route to warmer pools if we detect your traffic pattern.

[03:45] Aisha (Security): Where does request logging live and how long is it retained? Also key management?

[03:51] Alex: For hosted API we provide configurable retention; default short retention plus an option for extended logs under enterprise plan. Key management integrations with KMS/HSM are available for Private, and Hosted offers envelope encryption and customer-managed keys in some tiers. We'll share the SOC2 and encryption docs after the call.

[04:10] Priya: Back to retries — typical error classes we see: transient 5xx from infra, websocket disconnects, and rate-limit 429. For 5xx and websocket hiccups we recommend client retry with exponential backoff and resume logic; for 429 prefer token-based rate limiting handling: either slow down or use a fallback model with lower compute (quantized variant). We demo an automatic fallback policy in the console — it's a route-level config.

[04:50] Priya (demo): I'm switching to the Optimize tab — here the system suggests batching window changes based on observed throughput and recommends a quantized model for chat workloads with short ctx. It also shows expected token-cost delta and latency impact. For example, switching from fp16 to 4-bit Q4 reduces cost ~40% with a small median latency change.

[05:18] Jordan: That sounds promising, but we need to ensure quality doesn't drop for system prompts and long responses.

[05:24] Priya: Right — Optimize ties to evals. You can run A/B evals against a prompt suite and get quality regression alerts. The console will flag prompt failures and suggest rollback.

[05:40] Sofia: Could you explain more about prefix caching? How does it differ from sending the whole convo each time?

[05:47] Miguel: Prefix caching stores KV cache for model transformer layers so you don't re-send tokens. Instead you send a reference to cached prefix. It reduces both token cost and latency because you avoid re-encoding long history. Caveat: cache is model-variant dependent and subject to TTL.

[06:10] Devon: Do you support partial cache eviction and invalidation hooks?

[06:15] Priya: Yes — there are APIs to invalidate keys and you can set TTLs per route. We also expose cache hit/miss metrics in the console so you can tune retention.

[06:30] Alex: Let's simulate a failure and retry flow — Priya, can you break the connection and show reconnect?

[06:36] Priya (demo): I'm pausing the sandbox container now — you'll see the stream drop and the client auto-retries. (few seconds) The client attempted three retries with backoff, then resumed from token-offset 48 using KV checkpoint. You can also configure a policy to fallback to a smaller model variant automatically when retries exceed threshold.

[07:12] Jordan: If a retry causes a new generation with different randomness, how do we avoid duplicate messages to the user?

[07:20] Priya: Combine the client_message_id/idempotency_key with server side de-dupe window. The recommended UX is: if stream restarts, present a "resuming" state and only commit output once server returns final flag. Also you can request deterministic seed or low temperature to reduce variability for retries.

[07:55] Sofia: Any best-practice for token budgeting? We have mixed short and occasional long replies.

[08:02] Miguel: Use dynamic max_tokens per route — for short queries keep at 64 and allow bump for longer tasks. Also use streaming partials to show the user progressive output while you track token burn in the backend. Optimize will suggest average token counts and cost per 1k requests to help capacity planning.

[08:30] Aisha (Security): For compliance, do you support SSO and RBAC for console access and audit logs?

[08:37] Alex: Yes, SSO (SAML/OIDC) and fine-grained RBAC are available for enterprise, plus audit logs with immutable entries. We'll attach a short security checklist in the follow-up.

[08:50] Priya: Quick note — if you do private model deployment (VPC/private control plane) you can optionally keep logs off the hosted plane. But it requires more ops setup.

[09:05] Jordan: Can we try a short live smoke test? We'll send a list of sample prompts.

[09:10] Alex: Let's do a 10-message run using your sample prompts now. We'll watch the console metrics.

[09:14] (live demo)
[09:14] Priya: Sending prompts A1-A10, watch the stream telemetry.

[09:30] Jordan: I'm seeing median token latency ~120ms, p95 ~310ms for these small messages. That's within our goal. What's the best way to capture these numbers automatically?

[09:40] Miguel: We export per-request traces to your metrics endpoint and you can also plug the console tracing into Datadog or Prometheus. We'll send a sample dashboard.

[10:00] Sofia: About fallback to cheaper / quantized models, how automated is the quality gate?

[10:07] Priya: The console supports a rollout policy: threshold of error or quality regression triggers an automatic rollback or route-level fallback to cheaper model. But we strongly recommend A/B evaluation before broad rollout. Optimize will estimate quality drift on your prompt set.

[10:30] Devon: Any limits on concurrent streaming connections? We have thousands of peak concurrent users.

[10:36] Miguel: Hosted plans support high concurrency through autoscale; there are soft per-account concurrency quotas that we increase during pilot/contract negotiation. For very large scale we propose Dedicated or sharded routes.

[10:54] Aisha: Regarding data at rest — encryption specifics?

[10:58] Alex: Data at rest is AES-256; for hosted we offer server-side managed keys and customer-managed keys for enterprise tiers. We'll include KMS integration docs.

[11:12] Sofia: Any gotchas with streaming on mobile clients?

[11:18] Priya: Mobile networks can be flaky — recommend smaller chunk sizes and shorter keep-alive. Use reconnection logic with resume token. Also consider pre-warming small pools if you have many mobile bursts.

[11:40] Jordan: Let's discuss cost. If we start with hosted and later move to Dedicated, how does migration look?

[11:48] Alex: Migration is straightforward from a config/route perspective — same API surface. The difference is capacity contracts and routing policy. We can do a staged migration: pilot on hosted, then Dedicated reservation for production. There may be model variant differences if you want on-prem quantized variants; Redwood helps with the model onboarding.

[12:15] Sofia: Example of failure modes — any recommendation for user-facing fallback UX?

[12:22] Priya: Common pattern: show partial results, then if retries fail show a cached response or a short fallback message like "We're having trouble — try again in a moment" and log the event. For critical flows show degraded mode with limited feature set rather than full failure.

[12:45] Alex: Ok, quick recap and next steps.

[12:50] Alex (recap): 1) We'll send pricing and dedicated options (Alex) 2) Priya will push console recording and SDK snippets 3) Lumenix to run 1k-message smoke test and capture latency/cost metrics and confirm security checklist items 4) schedule pilot kickoff with infra (Jordan)

[13:20] Jordan: Sounds good. One more Q on observability — are spans correlated to tokens?

[13:26] Miguel: We emit per-request traces with token counts and latency breakdown (encode, decode, network). You can correlate on conversation_id.

[13:40] Aisha: For SOC2 and pen test reports — will you be able to share those?

[13:45] Alex: Yes, we'll share SOC2 + recent pen test summary under NDA; I'll include in the follow-up.

[13:58] Sofia: Great demo.

[14:02] Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the artifacts in the next 24 hours.
